angle: follow one message through the three services: a producer sends it to an SQS queue, which stores it in several Availability Zones before the producer moves on (1); consumers poll for it, best with long polling (2); a received message stays hidden until it is deleted or the visibility timeout ends (3); a standard queue can deliver it twice, so the consumer is idempotent (4), while a FIFO queue keeps order per message group and drops duplicates (5); a message that keeps failing moves to a dead-letter queue (6); the workers scale on the backlog per instance (7), or Lambda polls the queue for you (8). When many systems need the same message, an SNS topic pushes it to every subscriber (9); a queue per subscriber keeps each copy (10); a filter policy decides which copy each subscription gets (11). Events from AWS services and SaaS partners go to EventBridge, where a rule matches content and sends events to targets (12); SNS and EventBridge retry, then drop a delivery unless a dead-letter queue catches it (13); and resource-based policies decide who may send to a queue, a topic or a bus (14)

sections.heading: SQS stores each message in several Availability Zones before the sender moves on

plan.problem: A direct call makes the caller wait for the slowest part, and a failure on either side loses the request. A queue lets the sender finish before the receiver even starts.
trace: **Send and move on.** The producer sends a message, and SQS [stores the message in multiple availability zones] (sqs-send-stored-multi-az-before-ack) before it acknowledges it, so [no single computer, network, or AZ failure] (sqs-send-stored-multi-az-before-ack) makes the message inaccessible.

**Wait in the queue.** Producer and consumer exchange messages [without requiring each component to be concurrently available] (sns-faq-sqs-components-need-not-be-available-at-same-time); the number of messages a queue can store [is unlimited] (sqs-queue-backlog-unlimited).

**Absorb the spike.** SQS keeps [scaling transparently to handle any load increases] (sqs-scales-transparently-for-spikes) [without any provisioning instructions] (sqs-scales-transparently-for-spikes), so a burst makes the queue longer instead of failing requests.

**Expire if nobody processes it.** A queue keeps a message [4 days] (sqs-message-retention-default) by default; you can set [60 seconds] (sqs-message-retention-range) to [14 days] (sqs-message-retention-range). SQS [automatically deletes messages] (sqs-auto-deletes-after-retention-period) older than the [maximum message retention period] (sqs-auto-deletes-after-retention-period).
plan.table: Direct call or queue (columns: Question | Direct call | Through a queue): Receiver is down | the request fails | the message waits [until successfully processed or expired] (sqs-decision-keeps-until-processed); Traffic spike | the receiver is overloaded | the queue grows and consumers keep their pace: [fine-grained control over message processing rates] (sqs-decision-pull-model); What the caller gets back | the result | [an acknowledgment that a request has been registered] (sqs-wa-make-component-interactions-asynchronous). One link per fact per cell; cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Well-Architected asks for components that do not call each other directly but meet [through an intermediate durable storage layer]: write the link as [an intermediate durable storage layer] (sqs-wa-loose-coupling-via-intermediate-durable-layer), [such as an Amazon SQS queue] (sqs-wa-loose-coupling-via-intermediate-durable-layer). The durable middle lets each side fail or slow down alone.
plan.exam_signal: "the database cannot keep up during peaks" or "decouple the tiers" points to an SQS queue between the tiers; [buffering requests] (sqs-decision-typical-use) is a typical use.

sections.heading: Consumers poll the queue and long polling waits for messages to arrive

plan.problem: SQS does not push a message to anyone: consumers ask for messages. How they ask decides the cost and how soon they see a message.
trace: **Pull.** SQS uses a [Pull-based model] (sqs-decision-pull-model): consumers poll the queue.

**Short polling answers at once.** [Short polling (default)] (sqs-short-polling-is-default-immediate-response) [samples a subset of its servers] (sqs-short-polling-samples-subset-of-servers) and answers [even if no messages are found] (sqs-short-polling-is-default-immediate-response), so one call [might not return all of your messages] (sqs-short-polling-request-may-miss-messages).

**Long polling waits.** With a wait time [greater than 0, long polling is in effect] (sqs-long-polling-wait-greater-than-zero): the call [queries all servers for messages] (sqs-long-polling-queries-all-servers) and waits up to [20 seconds] (sqs-long-polling-max-wait) for one to arrive.

**Fewer empty answers.** Long polling lowers cost by [reducing the number of empty responses] (sqs-long-polling-reduces-empty-and-false-empty) and of [false empty responses] (sqs-long-polling-reduces-empty-and-false-empty).
**Take several at once.** One ReceiveMessage call [can process 10 messages at a time] (sqs-no-receive-message-batch-action).
plan.table: Short or long polling (columns: Question | Short polling | Long polling): Which servers it asks | a subset | all of them; Empty queue | it [returns immediately] (sqs-faq-long-polling-waits-for-message) | it waits [until a message arrives in the message queue] (sqs-faq-long-polling-waits-for-message) or the wait ends; Price of one call | the same: long polls are [billed exactly the same] (sqs-faq-long-polling-no-extra-charge).
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Asking a few servers is fast but can miss a message on the others; waiting lets SQS look on every server at no extra price per call.
plan.exam_signal: "reduce the number of empty receives" or "lower the cost of polling" points to long polling, which can [reduce the number of empty receives] (sqs-faq-long-polling-fewer-empty-receives-lower-cost).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: [long polling is preferable to short polling] (sqs-faq-long-polling-preferable-almost-all-cases) in [almost all cases] (sqs-faq-long-polling-preferable-almost-all-cases); the console default of [0 seconds] (sqs-console-receive-wait-time-default) [sets short polling] (sqs-console-receive-wait-time-default). Reference only, no sentence: [All AWS SDKs] (sqs-faq-sdk-default-20-second-long-poll) use [20-second long polls] (sqs-faq-sdk-default-20-second-long-poll); the HTTP timeout must be [longer than the WaitTimeSeconds parameter] (sqs-long-polling-http-timeout-longer-than-wait); batch actions handle [up to 10 messages at a time] (sqs-batch-up-to-10-messages-cost) and [cost the same as other Amazon SQS requests] (sqs-faq-batch-operations-cost-same-as-other-requests).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: use long polling, it waits for a message. The thing to watch is the client's HTTP timeout.
plan.stop_and_answer: A consumer calls ReceiveMessage in a tight loop on a queue that is often empty, and the bill shows millions of empty receives. Which queue setting lowers that, and does each call then cost more? Answer: set the receive message wait time above zero: [Any non-zero value sets long polling] (sqs-console-receive-wait-time-default). Each long poll is [billed exactly the same] (sqs-faq-long-polling-no-extra-charge) as a short poll, and there are far fewer of them.

sections.heading: A received message stays hidden until it is deleted or the timeout ends

plan.problem: Receiving a message does not remove it. SQS must keep other consumers away while one consumer works, and bring the message back if that consumer fails.
trace: **Receive.** After a receive, [it remains in the queue] (sqs-receive-keeps-message-hidden) but is [temporarily invisible to other consumers] (sqs-receive-keeps-message-hidden).

**Hide for the visibility timeout.** The timeout is [30 seconds] (sqs-visibility-timeout-default) by default; you can set it from [0 seconds] (sqs-visibility-timeout-range) to [12 hours] (sqs-visibility-timeout-range).

**Delete when done.** The consumer deletes the message with the [receipt handle] (sqs-faq-receipt-handle-required-to-delete) of the receive, which you [must provide when deleting the message] (sqs-faq-receipt-handle-required-to-delete): [You explicitly delete messages] (sqs-manual-delete-after-processing).

**Come back on failure.** Without a delete, the message [becomes visible again in the queue] (sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again) and can be [retrieved by another consumer] (sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again), so messages [aren't lost even if the initial processing fails] (sqs-failed-processing-message-not-lost).

**Extend long work.** The [ChangeMessageVisibility action] (sqs-change-message-visibility-extend-shorten) can [extend or shorten the timeout as needed] (sqs-change-message-visibility-extend-shorten) for one message.
plan.table: Visibility timeout compared with the processing time (columns: Timeout | What happens): shorter than the processing | [a duplicate message is received by another consumer] (sqs-visibility-timeout-too-short-gives-duplicate); a little longer | one consumer finishes, and a failed message returns soon; far longer | after a failure you [wait for a relatively long time] (sqs-visibility-timeout-too-long-delays-retry). Truth table: one row per case, the result in the last column.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? SQS cannot tell a crashed consumer from a slow one. A timer is the only signal it has, so the timer must fit the work.
plan.exam_signal: "some messages are processed twice" together with long processing points to a visibility timeout that ends while the [original consumer is still working on the message] (sqs-visibility-timeout-too-short-gives-duplicate).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A short visibility timeout is not the safe choice. If it ends while the consumer still works, [a duplicate message is received by another consumer] (sqs-visibility-timeout-too-short-gives-duplicate). <!-- trap: messaging-trap-short-visibility-safer -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: the 12-hour ceiling. Extending the timeout [does not reset the 12 hour maximum] (sqs-visibility-timeout-extend-no-reset), which counts from the receive. Set the timeout [longer than the AWS SDK read timeout] (sqs-visibility-timeout-longer-than-sdk-read-timeout). Contrast: a delay queue hides a message [hidden when it is first added to queue] (sqs-delay-queue-hidden-at-add-visibility-after-receive), the visibility timeout [only after it is consumed from the queue] (sqs-delay-queue-hidden-at-add-visibility-after-receive). At most 60 words.

The reveal does not repeat the minutes.

sections.heading: A standard queue can deliver a message twice so consumers must be idempotent

plan.problem: A standard queue scales by keeping copies of each message on several servers. The price is that a copy can come back.
trace: **Keep copies.** If a server that holds a copy is down at delete time, the copy [isn't deleted on the server that is unavailable] (sqs-copies-on-multiple-servers-cause-duplicates), and [you might get that message copy again] (sqs-copies-on-multiple-servers-cause-duplicates).

**Deliver at least once.** A standard queue gives [at-least-once message delivery] (sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates): [more than one copy of a message] (sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates) can arrive, and [messages may occasionally arrive out of order] (sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates).
**Try to keep order.** It makes a [best-effort attempt to maintain the order] (sqs-standard-best-effort-ordering), nothing more.
**Scale almost without limit.** In return it supports a [nearly unlimited number of API calls per second] (sqs-standard-throughput-nearly-unlimited).

**Make the consumer idempotent.** [Design your applications to be idempotent] (sqs-copies-on-multiple-servers-cause-duplicates): consumers [keep track of each token received] (sqs-consumers-keep-idempotency-tokens-ignore-duplicates) and skip a token they have seen.
plan.table: What a duplicate does (columns: Consumer action | Not idempotent | Idempotent): set status to done | same result | same result; add a credit to a balance | the balance is wrong | it skips a message ID it already processed; send an email | the customer gets two | it checks a record of sent messages. Plain words, no links (example rows).
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Copies on several servers keep the queue available and fast. An idempotent service makes [multiple identical requests has the same effect] (sqs-idempotent-service-same-effect-as-single-request) [as making a single request] (sqs-idempotent-service-same-effect-as-single-request): write it as one sentence that reads naturally around the two links, or link only the second display.
plan.exam_signal: "nearly unlimited throughput" and "order does not matter" point to a standard queue with idempotent consumers; it supports a [nearly unlimited number of API calls per second] (sqs-standard-throughput-nearly-unlimited).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a standard queue may repeat a message. The thing to watch is code that charges twice.
plan.stop_and_answer: A consumer adds a credit to a customer account for each message. One message produced two credits. Is the queue broken? Answer: no; a standard queue gives [at-least-once message delivery] (sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates). The consumer must record each message's ID and skip IDs it has seen: consumers [keep track of each token received] (sqs-consumers-keep-idempotency-tokens-ignore-duplicates).

sections.heading: A FIFO queue keeps order inside each message group and drops duplicates

plan.problem: Some work must happen once and in order: a debit before the refund of the same account. A FIFO queue gives order and no duplicates, but per message group and at a lower rate.
trace: **Name the group.** Every message carries a group ID: you [associate a message group ID with each message] (sqs-fifo-message-group-id-required); a message [sent without a group ID, the action fails] (sqs-fifo-message-group-id-required).

**Keep order in the group.** [Within a message group ID] (sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group) messages are [sent and received in strict order] (sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group); while one is in flight, no other message comes [from the same message group ID] (sqs-fifo-in-flight-blocks-same-group) [until the first message is deleted] (sqs-fifo-in-flight-blocks-same-group).
**Run groups in parallel.** A FIFO queue allows [parallel processing of messages] (sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel) [across different message group IDs] (sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel).

**Drop duplicates.** A second message with the same deduplication ID within the [5 minute deduplication interval] (sqs-fifo-deduplication-interval-5-minutes) is a duplicate, and [only one copy is delivered] (sqs-fifo-deduplication-interval-5-minutes). Content-based deduplication uses a [SHA-256 hash] (sqs-fifo-content-based-dedup-hash-body-only) of the body, [but not the attributes of the message] (sqs-fifo-content-based-dedup-hash-body-only).

**Accept a rate.** By default a FIFO queue supports up to [300 messages per second] (sqs-faq-fifo-default-throughput-3000-with-batching-300-without), or [3,000 messages per second with batching] (sqs-faq-fifo-default-throughput-3000-with-batching-300-without).
plan.table: Which message group ID (columns: Group ID | Order | Parallel work): one ID for every message | one order for the whole queue: [use a single message group ID] (sqs-fifo-single-group-for-strict-order) | one consumer at a time; the customer ID | order for each customer | many customers at once; a new ID for each message | no useful order | as much as the queue allows. Truth table.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Order needs one consumer at a time for a group: FIFO queues do not serve a group to [more than one consumer at a time] (sqs-faq-fifo-same-group-one-consumer-at-a-time). Small groups keep that limit small.
plan.exam_signal: "in the order they were sent" with "exactly once" points to a FIFO queue, which gives [exactly-once processing] (sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A FIFO queue does not keep one order across all groups. [Messages with different message group IDs] (sqs-fifo-no-order-across-groups) [may arrive or be processed out of order] (sqs-fifo-no-order-across-groups). <!-- trap: messaging-trap-fifo-global-order -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: fair queues in a standard queue. Since July 2025, fairness is [applied automatically in all Amazon SQS standard queues] (sqs-fair-queues-automatic-no-consumer-change) to messages that carry a group ID; it [mitigates the noisy-neighbor impact] (sqs-fair-queues-noisy-neighbor-mitigation) of one busy tenant. There the group ID is [used only as a tenant identifier] (sqs-fair-queues-groupid-is-tenant-id-no-ordering) and [does not enforce message ordering] (sqs-fair-queues-groupid-is-tenant-id-no-ordering). At most 60 words; 'July 2025' may link [July 21, 2025] (sqs-change-fair-queues-standard-2025) instead.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: the name [must end with the .fifo suffix] (sqs-fifo-queue-name-suffix), and you [cannot convert an existing standard queue] (sqs-cannot-convert-standard-queue-to-fifo) to FIFO. Reference only: high throughput mode quotas are volatile (sqs-fifo-ht-top-regions-70000-tps); no sentence.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: FIFO keeps order per group, with no duplicates. The thing to watch is the group ID you choose.
plan.stop_and_answer: A FIFO queue holds payment events. The group ID is the payment type, card or bank, so one slow card payment holds up every card payment. Which group ID keeps each customer's events in order and lets customers run in parallel? Answer: the customer ID. Order holds [within a message group ID] (sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group), and different groups allow [parallel processing of messages] (sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel).

sections.heading: After too many failed receives SQS moves a message to a dead-letter queue

plan.problem: A poison-pill message fails every time. Without a limit it comes back again and again, uses consumers and hides real failures.
trace: **Count the receives.** A redrive policy sets maxReceiveCount: the [number of times a consumer can receive] (sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) a message [before it is moved to a dead-letter queue] (sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning).

**Move it aside.** When the receive count [exceeds the maxReceiveCount] (sqs-faq-dlq-message-moved-when-receive-count-exceeds-max), SQS moves the message [with its original message ID] (sqs-faq-dlq-message-moved-when-receive-count-exceeds-max).

**Match type and place.** The dead-letter queue of a FIFO queue [must also be a FIFO queue] (sqs-dlq-type-must-match-source-queue-type), and that of a standard queue [must also be a standard queue] (sqs-dlq-type-must-match-source-queue-type). It is in the [same AWS account and Region] (sqs-dlq-same-account-and-region).

**Mind the clock.** In a standard queue [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged] (sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged) by the move, so set the dead-letter queue's retention [longer than the retention period] (sqs-dlq-retention-longer-than-source-queue) of the source. In a FIFO queue [the enqueue timestamp resets] (sqs-dlq-fifo-enqueue-timestamp-resets).

**Fix, then redrive.** After you fix the consumer, you can [redrive the messages from your dead-letter queue] (sqs-faq-dlq-redrive-back-to-source-queue) [to the source queue] (sqs-faq-dlq-redrive-back-to-source-queue).
plan.table: Choosing maxReceiveCount (columns: Setting | Effect): a low count | a short glitch can send a good message aside; a few receives | short glitches retry, a poison-pill message leaves soon; a queue that Lambda reads | AWS advises [at least 5] (lambda-sqs-dlq-maxreceivecount-5); no redrive policy | the message returns until the retention period deletes it. Four rows; cut row 1 first if over budget.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Setting failures aside keeps the main queue moving. SQS offers [dead-letter queues and poison-pill management] (sqs-faq-hosted-queue-between-microservices-dlq-poison-pill) as common middleware.
plan.exam_signal: "isolate messages that cannot be processed" points to a dead-letter queue, which receives messages when the consumer is [unable to consume the messages successfully] (sqs-faq-dlq-definition-isolate-unprocessable-messages).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A moved message does not start a fresh retention period in a standard queue: [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged] (sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged). Set the dead-letter queue's retention [longer than the retention period] (sqs-dlq-retention-longer-than-source-queue) of the source queue. <!-- trap: messaging-trap-dlq-fresh-retention -->
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: the rules of a redrive. A [redrive task resets the retention period] (sqs-redrive-resets-retention-and-assigns-new-id), and redriven messages are [considered new messages] (sqs-redrive-resets-retention-and-assigns-new-id). It moves them [starting with the oldest message] (sqs-redrive-oldest-first-order); SQS [doesn't support filtering and modifying messages] (sqs-redrive-no-filter-or-modify) on the way. A FIFO queue with a dead-letter queue can [break the exact order of messages or operations] (sqs-dlq-with-fifo-can-break-order). At most 60 words.
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence: alarm on [use the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric] (sns-dlq-alarm-on-visible-messages-not-messages-sent) of the dead-letter queue, because the [NumberOfMessagesSent metric is not suitable] (sns-dlq-alarm-on-visible-messages-not-messages-sent); a redrive allow policy can deny use: [If you specify denyAll] (sqs-dlq-denyall-blocks-use-as-dlq).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: after a few failed tries, the message moves aside. The thing to watch is the dead-letter queue's retention.
plan.stop_and_answer: A FIFO queue named orders.fifo gets a redrive policy that points to a standard queue named orders-dlq. Will SQS accept it? Answer: no; the dead-letter queue of a FIFO queue [must also be a FIFO queue] (sqs-dlq-type-must-match-source-queue-type).

sections.heading: Workers scale on the backlog per instance and not on queue length

plan.problem: Workers behind a queue must grow when messages wait too long and shrink when the queue drains. CPU and the raw queue length both give the wrong signal.
trace: **Read the queue.** [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible] (sqs-metric-visible-messages-is-backlog) counts messages [available for retrieval and processing] (sqs-metric-visible-messages-is-backlog): the backlog. [ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible] (sqs-metric-not-visible-messages-is-in-flight) counts in-flight messages. [ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage] (sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag) gives the age of the [oldest unprocessed message in the queue] (sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag).

**Divide by the fleet.** The queue length [might not change proportionally] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the group size, so use the [backlog per instance] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance): visible messages divided by [GroupInServiceInstances] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math), built with [metric math] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-metric-math-instead-of-custom).

**Set the target.** The target tracking target is the [acceptable backlog per instance] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance): take the acceptable wait and [divide it by the average time] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-acceptable-backlog-per-instance-target) one message takes.

**Protect long jobs.** A message that is not finished when its instance ends is [returned to the SQS queue] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-unprocessed-messages-return); [use instance scale-in protection] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-unprocessed-messages-return) for long work.
**Add consumers.** More consumers give [essentially linear gains in queue throughput] (sqs-horizontal-scaling-linear-gain).
plan.table: Scaling metric for queue workers (columns: Metric | Result): average CPU | for batch work [100% CPU utilization is expected and should not be your primary metric] (ec2-auto-scaling-wa-queue-depth-metric-for-batch-work); visible messages alone | it [might not change proportionally] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional) to the group size; backlog per instance | moves with the group size, so target tracking can hold it (plain words). Cells at most 15 words: the CPU cell is the display plus 'for batch work' (14 words).
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? What one worker faces is the backlog divided by the workers. That number falls when the group grows, so a target tracking policy can steer it.
plan.exam_signal: "scale the workers on the number of messages in the queue" points to target tracking on backlog per instance, which uses the [acceptable backlog per instance] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance) as its target.
plan.startup_example: > **Startup example:** Callvale's convert queue feeds conversion workers in an Auto Scaling group that runs from zero to 40 instances. The group tracks the backlog per instance, so it grows in the morning and empties at night. (at most 30 words; 40 is worker_group_max of stage 2; write 'zero' as a word)
plan.body_extras: Reference only (B-list): a standard queue holds [approximately 120,000 in flight messages] (sqs-in-flight-standard-limit); at that point short polling [returns the OverLimit error message] (sqs-in-flight-standard-limit-short-vs-long-polling). Amazon ECS services scale the same way, on the [scale on the *backlog per task*] (ecs-sqs-scale-on-backlog-per-task): copy that display exactly with its asterisks only if a writer needs it; it is not planned in prose.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: scale workers on the messages waiting per worker. The thing to watch is long jobs during scale-in.
plan.stop_and_answer: A group of four workers faces two thousand visible messages, and the target is a backlog of one hundred per instance. Will target tracking add workers? Answer: yes; the backlog per instance is visible messages divided by [GroupInServiceInstances] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math), which is five times the target here. Numbers in the prompt are words, so the reveal needs no number with a unit.

sections.heading: Lambda polls the queue for you and the queue decides the retries

plan.problem: With Lambda as the consumer you write no polling code. The retry rules still belong to the queue.
trace: **Lambda polls.** SQS reaches Lambda through an [Event source mapping] (lambda-trigger-sqs-esm): [Lambda handles the polling] (lambda-esm-lambda-polls-source) and invokes the function.

**Batch the messages.** The batch size defaults to [10] (lambda-sqs-batch-size): [For standard queues, the maximum is 10,000] (lambda-sqs-batch-size); [For FIFO queues, the maximum is 10] (lambda-sqs-batch-size).

**Scale with the backlog.** Lambda starts with [five batches at a time with five concurrent invocations] (lambda-sqs-scaling-5-batches-300-per-minute-1250) and adds [up to 300 more concurrent invokes per minute] (lambda-sqs-scaling-5-batches-300-per-minute-1250); maximum concurrency caps one source [between 2 and 1,000] (lambda-sqs-max-concurrency-range).

**Fail through the queue.** A failed batch returns by the queue's [visibility timeout and redrive policy] (lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue). With a [partial batch response] (lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), Lambda can [make only the failed messages visible again] (lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response).

**Size the timeout.** Give the queue a visibility timeout of [at least six times] (lambda-sqs-visibility-six-times-timeout) the function timeout; the function timeout [must be less than or equal to] (lambda-sqs-timeout-not-above-visibility) the visibility timeout.
plan.table: Where each setting lives (columns: Setting | Where you set it): retries and failed messages | on the source queue: its [visibility timeout and redrive policy] (lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue); batch size and maximum concurrency | on the event source mapping; permission to read | the execution role, with [sqs:ReceiveMessage] (lambda-sqs-execution-role-read-permissions).
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? The queue already hides, counts and sets aside messages; Lambda reuses those rules instead of adding its own.
plan.exam_signal: "process queue messages without managing servers" points to a Lambda function with an SQS event source mapping, where [Lambda handles the polling] (lambda-esm-lambda-polls-source).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** One failed message does not mean one retried message. Without [ReportBatchItemFailures] (lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response), the whole batch returns to the queue; with it, Lambda can [make only the failed messages visible again] (lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response). <!-- trap: messaging-trap-lambda-retries-failed-only -->
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain: event source mappings [process each event at least once] (lambda-esm-at-least-once), so the function must be idempotent, as in subsection 4. Chapter 18 owns the details (<!-- xref: 18 event source mappings and partial batch responses -->); this subsection names no concurrency quota beyond the trace.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Lambda polls, and the queue keeps the retry rules. The thing to watch is the visibility timeout.
plan.stop_and_answer: A function has a timeout longer than the visibility timeout of its SQS queue. What happens when you create the event source mapping? Answer: Lambda [returns an error] (lambda-sqs-timeout-not-above-visibility): the function timeout [must be less than or equal to] (lambda-sqs-timeout-not-above-visibility) the visibility timeout.

sections.heading: An SNS topic pushes each published message to all its subscribers

plan.problem: A queue gives each message to one consumer. When many systems need the same message now, the sender would have to call each one. A topic does that for the sender.
trace: **Publish once.** [Publishers communicate asynchronously with subscribers] (sns-publishers-send-to-topic-asynchronously) through a topic.

**Store before the answer.** SNS keeps [multiple copies (to disk)] (sns-faq-durable-storage-multiple-copies-multiple-azs) in [multiple Availability Zones before acknowledging receipt] (sns-faq-durable-storage-multiple-copies-multiple-azs).

**Push to every subscriber.** SNS delivers to [all applicable subscribers] (sns-faq-publish-triggers-delivery-to-all-subscribers) with a [Push-based model] (sns-decision-push-model), which [removes the need to check or “poll”] (sns-push-mechanism-no-polling).

**Reach applications and people.** Subscribers include [delivery streams, Lambda functions, Amazon SQS queues] (sns-a2a-subscriber-types) and [mobile applications, mobile phone numbers, and email addresses] (sns-a2p-subscriber-types); SNS [invokes AWS Lambda functions asynchronously] (sns-lambda-invoked-asynchronously).
**Keep nothing afterwards.** [Messages are not persisted] (sns-decision-no-persistence), and a published message [cannot be recalled] (sns-faq-published-message-cannot-be-recalled).
plan.table: Queue or topic (columns: Question | SQS queue | SNS topic): who gets a message | one consumer: SQS has [a single subscriber typically] (sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss) | every subscriber; how it arrives | consumers poll | it is pushed; a receiver is offline | the message waits | delivery is retried, then [Messages are not persisted] (sns-decision-no-persistence) means it is gone.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Push removes polling from many receivers and keeps the delay short: SNS [typical latency] (sns-faq-sns-typical-latency-under-30-milliseconds) is [under 30 milliseconds] (sns-faq-sns-typical-latency-under-30-milliseconds).
plan.exam_signal: "notify several systems at the same time" or "fanout" points to an SNS topic, often used for [fanout notifications] (sns-decision-typical-use).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain: subscribers can see [occasional, duplicate messages] (sns-faq-subscriber-may-receive-duplicates) and [out-of-order messages at the subscriber end] (sns-faq-order-attempted-but-network-issues-can-reorder) on a standard topic. Reference only: a standard topic takes [12,500,000 per topic] (sns-quota-subscriptions-per-topic) subscriptions by default; the default message size [256 KiB] (sns-message-size-default-256kib) is volatile.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a topic pushes one message to every subscriber. The thing to watch is a subscriber that is offline.
plan.stop_and_answer: A topic has an email subscription and a Lambda subscription. The function is deleted by mistake for a week. Does the email subscriber still get each message? Answer: yes; SNS delivers to [all applicable subscribers] (sns-faq-publish-triggers-delivery-to-all-subscribers) one by one. The messages for the deleted function are not kept, because [Messages are not persisted] (sns-decision-no-persistence).

sections.heading: Queues subscribed to a topic give each consumer its own durable copy

plan.problem: SNS alone loses a message when a subscriber is offline; SQS alone gives each message to one consumer. Together they give every consumer its own copy that waits.
trace: **Subscribe one queue per consumer.** Subscribe [multiple SQS standard queues to the SNS topic] (sns-faq-fanout-identical-messages-to-multiple-sqs-queues); SNS then [sends the message to each subscribed queue] (sns-publish-sends-message-to-each-subscribed-queue).

**Let the queue accept the topic.** You must [set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue] (sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic) that allows messages [sent from the Amazon SNS topic] (sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic); the [aws:SourceArn condition] (sns-queue-policy-sourcearn-limits-to-one-topic) admits that one topic.

**Confirm only across accounts.** A queue and topic of the [same AWS account] (sns-faq-same-account-sqs-subscription-needs-no-opt-in) need no [opt-in] (sns-faq-same-account-sqs-subscription-needs-no-opt-in); a subscriber who does not own the queue [must confirm the subscription] (sns-cross-account-non-owner-must-confirm-subscription).

**Each queue keeps its copy.** The messages [persist in an Amazon SQS queue] (sns-sqs-together-instant-notice-and-later-processing), which prevents loss [when subscribers are offline] (sns-with-sqs-prevents-loss-for-offline-subscribers).

**Unwrap if you want.** Each copy holds [metadata about the message in a JSON document] (sns-sqs-envelope-contains-subject-message-metadata); with raw message delivery, [any Amazon SNS metadata is stripped] (sns-raw-delivery-sqs-strips-sns-metadata).
plan.table: Pairing topic and queue types (columns: Need | Topic | Queues): every consumer, any order | standard topic | standard queues; ordered fan-out | FIFO topic, for [consistent end-to-end message ordering] (sns-faq-fifo-topic-to-sqs-fifo-queue-end-to-end-ordering) | FIFO queues; ordered topic, consumers that accept duplicates | FIFO topic | standard queues, which [lets you lower costs] (sns-fifo-standard-queue-subscriber-lowers-cost). Truth table.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Each queue decouples one consumer from the publisher and from the other consumers: a slow indexer no longer slows the webhooks. The integration guide names this combination: events go to a queue [as a buffer for downstream consumers] (sqs-decision-combine-buffer-for-consumers).
plan.exam_signal: "every service must get every message, even while it is down" points to SNS fan-out to SQS queues; a common pattern is to [publish messages to Amazon SQS queues] (sns-faq-common-pattern-sns-publishes-to-sqs-queues).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** A subscription alone does not let SNS write to the queue. You must [set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue] (sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic) that allows the topic. <!-- trap: messaging-trap-subscribe-without-queue-policy -->
plan.try_it: messaging-t03: one sentence ('Send one message to two queues through a topic, and see what a missing queue policy does.'), then See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: messaging-t03 -->
plan.diagram: messaging-fanout after the trace (text fixed in diagrams); its alt and caption count toward words_all_in.
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence: an SNS FIFO topic [can't deliver messages to customer managed endpoints] (sns-fifo-topic-cannot-deliver-to-customer-managed-endpoints); Lambda triggers take [standard SNS topics only] (sns-lambda-triggers-standard-topics-only), so FIFO fan-out to functions goes through queues: [subscribe Amazon SQS FIFO or standard queues] (sns-fifo-to-lambda-needs-sqs-in-between).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: one topic, and one queue for each consumer. The thing to watch is each queue's access policy.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company adds a third queue to its order topic for a new audit service. The audit service is down for a day after launch. Are that day's orders lost for the audit service? Answer: no; its subscribed queue keeps them: the messages [persist in an Amazon SQS queue] (sns-sqs-together-instant-notice-and-later-processing) until the service reads them, within the queue's retention period.

sections.heading: A filter policy decides which messages reach each subscription

plan.problem: Not every subscriber needs every message. Without a filter, each consumer receives everything and throws most of it away.
trace: **Everything by default.** A subscriber [receives every message that's published to the topic] (sns-filter-default-every-message).
**Add a filter policy.** For a subset, [assign a filter policy to the topic subscription] (sns-filter-default-every-message).

**Choose what it reads.** The policy reads [message attributes (default setting)] (sns-filter-scope-attributes-default-or-body), or the body: [Applies the filter policy to the message body] (sns-filter-scope-attributes-default-or-body), which must be a [well-formed JSON object] (sns-filter-body-scope-needs-json-payload).

**Match or skip.** SNS sends a message when its attributes or body [satisfy the conditions specified in the filter policy] (sns-filter-nonmatching-message-not-sent); otherwise it [doesn't send the message to that subscriber] (sns-filter-nonmatching-message-not-sent).
**Allow time for a change.** A new or changed policy needs [up to 15 minutes] (sns-filter-policy-change-up-to-15-minutes) to take full effect.
plan.table: Where to filter (columns: Option | Effort and cost): no filter, the consumer discards | every consumer receives and pays for every message; filter policy on attributes | [Attribute-based message filtering is free] (sns-pricing-attribute-filtering-free); filter policy on the body | billed by the [total amount of outbound payload data scanned] (sns-pricing-attribute-filtering-free); a function between topic and queue | code to write, run and pay for. The two pricing links point to a volatile fact: allowed in prose, never a question key.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? Filtering at the subscription keeps publishers simple: they publish once, and each subscription states what it wants.
plan.exam_signal: "each subscriber should receive only the messages it needs" points to subscription filter policies, with which subscribers [selectively receive only a subset] (sns-faq-message-filtering-subscribers-receive-subset).
plan.exam_trap_text: > **Exam trap:** You need no function to filter a topic's messages. The subscriber can [assign a filter policy to the topic subscription] (sns-filter-default-every-message). <!-- trap: messaging-trap-filter-needs-function -->
plan.body_extras: Reference only, no sentence: a policy has a [maximum of five keys] (sns-filter-policy-max-keys); with filtering, a FIFO topic gives [at-most-once delivery] (sns-fifo-exactly-once-lost-with-filtering).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: each subscription can filter its own messages. The thing to watch is the delay after a change.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team adds a filter policy so that the EU queue gets only EU orders. A minute later the queue still receives US orders. Is the policy wrong? Answer: not yet a sign of an error; a change needs [up to 15 minutes] (sns-filter-policy-change-up-to-15-minutes) to take full effect.

sections.heading: An EventBridge rule matches event content and sends each match to its targets

plan.problem: Many events come from AWS services and SaaS applications, not from your code, and consumers want them by content. EventBridge routes events with rules instead of subscriptions.
trace: **Land on a bus.** Every account has a [default event bus] (eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events) that [automatically receives events from AWS services] (eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events). Your own events can go to buses [called custom event buses] (eventbridge-custom-bus-your-own-events); [partner event buses] (eventbridge-partner-bus-receives-saas-events) [receive events from SaaS partners] (eventbridge-partner-bus-receives-saas-events).

**Share one shape.** Events are [represented as JSON objects] (eventbridge-events-are-json-with-same-top-level-fields) with [the same top-level fields] (eventbridge-events-are-json-with-same-top-level-fields).

**Match a pattern.** A rule [matches incoming events for a given event bus] (eventbridge-faq-rule-matches-events-on-a-bus-and-routes-to-targets). sections.heading: Failed deliveries are retried and then dropped unless a dead-letter queue catches them

plan.problem: SNS and EventBridge push. When the receiver is down they cannot wait forever, so each has a retry rule and an optional dead-letter queue.
trace: **SNS retries in phases.** SNS runs a [4-phase retry policy] (sns-faq-four-phase-delivery-retry-policy). To SQS and Lambda it tries [100,015 times] (sns-retry-aws-managed-total-attempts) [over 23 days] (sns-retry-aws-managed-total-attempts); to email, SMS and mobile push, [50 attempts] (sns-retry-customer-managed-total-attempts) [over 6 hours] (sns-retry-customer-managed-total-attempts).

**SNS then drops.** When the policy ends, SNS [stops retrying the delivery and discards the message] (sns-retry-exhausted-discards-unless-dlq), unless [a dead-letter queue is attached to the subscription] (sns-retry-exhausted-discards-unless-dlq).

**EventBridge retries for a day.** By default it retries for [24 hours] (eventbridge-retry-default-24h-185-attempts) and [up to 185 times] (eventbridge-retry-default-24h-185-attempts); you can change the [length of time it tries] (eventbridge-retry-length-and-attempts-set-per-target) for each target.
**Some errors skip the retries.** A missing permission or a deleted target sends the event on [without any retry attempts] (eventbridge-some-errors-skip-retries).

**EventBridge then drops.** After the last attempt [the event is dropped] (eventbridge-retry-exhausted-event-dropped), unless you [configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ)] (eventbridge-retry-exhausted-event-dropped); it is one of the [standard Amazon SQS queues] (eventbridge-dlq-is-standard-sqs-queue).
plan.table: Retries and dead-letter queues (columns: Service | Default retry | Where the dead-letter queue goes): SQS | the message returns after each visibility timeout | on the source queue, after the [number of times a consumer can receive] (sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning); SNS | phases that depend on the endpoint type | on each subscription: [attached to an Amazon SNS subscription] (sns-dlq-attached-to-subscription-not-topic); EventBridge | [24 hours] (eventbridge-retry-default-24h-185-attempts) | on each target, and you [can't use a FIFO queue for a DLQ] (eventbridge-dlq-fifo-not-supported). Truth table.
plan.why: Why does AWS work this way? A push service that kept every message forever would be a queue. It hands long-term keeping to SQS, through the dead-letter queue.

To keep events, add an archive.] (eventbridge-classic-bus-does-not-retain-events) An archive [stores events in an archive indefinitely] (eventbridge-archive-retention-indefinite-by-default) unless you set days. sections.plan: Ten items of D12 from faq below: '**FAQ <n>.** <question>?', then a reveal with the short answer (with its link) and the AWS quote block (the quote field, copied exactly, then the link line). At most 450 words (aim 430).

traps.belief: Receiving a message removes it from the queue.
traps.truth: The message stays in the queue, hidden from other consumers, until the consumer deletes it; if it is not deleted before the visibility timeout ends, it becomes visible again.

traps.belief: When several services poll one queue, each service gets every message.
traps.truth: A queue typically gives each message to a single consumer; to give every service its own copy, subscribe one SQS queue per service to an SNS topic.

traps.belief: An SNS topic keeps messages until an offline subscriber comes back.
traps.truth: SNS does not persist messages: it retries the delivery, then discards the message unless a dead-letter queue is attached to the subscription. Subscribe an SQS queue to keep messages for an offline consumer.

traps.belief: A standard queue delivers each message exactly once and in the order it was sent.
traps.truth: A standard queue gives at-least-once delivery: more than one copy of a message can arrive, and messages can arrive out of order, so consumers must be idempotent.

traps.belief: An EventBridge event bus keeps its events, so a target can read or replay them later.
traps.truth: A Classic event bus does not retain events and EventBridge does not persist them; to keep events and send them again, add an archive and start a replay.

traps.belief: A short visibility timeout is the safe choice, because a failed message comes back sooner.
traps.truth: If the visibility timeout ends while the consumer still works, another consumer receives a duplicate of the message; set the timeout longer than the processing time.

traps.belief: A FIFO queue keeps one order across all of its messages, whatever their message group IDs.
traps.truth: Order is strict only within one message group ID; messages with different group IDs may arrive or be processed out of order relative to one another.

traps.belief: A message that moves to a dead-letter queue starts a new retention period there.
traps.truth: In a standard queue the enqueue timestamp does not change when the message moves, so the dead-letter queue needs a retention period longer than the source queue's.

traps.belief: When one message of a batch that Lambda reads from SQS fails, Lambda retries only that message.
traps.truth: Retries go through the queue: without a partial batch response the failed batch becomes visible again; with ReportBatchItemFailures, Lambda makes only the failed messages visible again.

traps.belief: Subscribing an SQS queue to an SNS topic is enough for the messages to arrive.
traps.truth: The queue's access policy must allow the topic to send messages; the aws:SourceArn condition limits that permission to the one topic.

traps.belief: To send only some of a topic's messages to one subscriber, you put a Lambda function between the topic and the subscriber.
traps.truth: A subscriber receives every message by default; a filter policy on its subscription makes SNS send it only the messages that match.

traps.belief: An SNS dead-letter queue is set once on the topic and catches the failed deliveries of every subscriber.
traps.truth: An SNS dead-letter queue is attached to a subscription, not to the topic, because deliveries happen at the subscription level; without one, SNS discards a message when its retries end.

traps.belief: An IAM policy in the sender's own account is enough to send messages to a queue in another account.
traps.truth: The queue's access policy must also allow that principal; identity-based policies alone are not sufficient for cross-account access to a queue, whose default policy allows only the owner.

traps.belief: SQS moves a message that was not deleted to a dead-letter queue by itself when the visibility timeout ends.
traps.truth: A message moves to a dead-letter queue only through a redrive policy, after the number of receives that maxReceiveCount sets; until then it becomes visible again in the source queue.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-1 for messaging-q003)

traps.belief: An SNS topic can take events from SaaS partner applications directly, so SNS and EventBridge are interchangeable for SaaS events.
traps.truth: EventBridge is the only event-based service that integrates directly with third-party SaaS partners; SNS would need extra parts in front of the topic.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-1 for messaging-q013)

traps.belief: The dead-letter queue of an EventBridge rule target keeps the events that the target processed wrongly, so they can be sent again.
traps.truth: A target's dead-letter queue stores only events that could not be delivered; to process delivered events again, archive them and start a replay.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-1 for messaging-q017)

traps.belief: An SQS delay queue or a message timer can hold a message for hours or days before consumers see it.
traps.truth: Delay queues and message timers delay a message for at most 15 minutes; for longer or one-time scheduling, EventBridge Scheduler is the recommended solution.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-1 for messaging-q021)

traps.belief: A longer visibility timeout stops a message that fails every time from coming back to the consumers.
traps.truth: A longer visibility timeout only makes the consumers wait longer before the next attempt; a redrive policy moves the message to a dead-letter queue after the number of receives that maxReceiveCount sets.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-2 for messaging-q009)

traps.belief: A FIFO queue drops every duplicate of a message, however late the duplicate arrives.
traps.truth: A FIFO queue treats a message as a duplicate only inside the 5 minute deduplication interval; duplicates that arrive later need an idempotent consumer that keeps track of each token.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-2 for messaging-q004)

traps.belief: To react when an AWS resource changes, you write code that polls its API on a schedule or reads its logs.
traps.truth: AWS services send their events to the default event bus automatically; an EventBridge rule matches the events and sends each match to its targets.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-2 for messaging-q006)

traps.belief: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible shows the messages that are waiting in the queue.
traps.truth: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible counts in-flight messages that were received but not yet deleted; ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible is the waiting backlog, and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage shows how long the oldest message has waited.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-2 for messaging-q008 and messaging-q010)

traps.belief: An SNS topic sends every message to every subscriber, so a subscriber that needs only some messages needs its own topic or an EventBridge rule.
traps.truth: A filter policy on a subscription makes SNS send that subscriber only the messages that match; the publishers and the topic do not change.
traps.placed_in: question distractors only (added by questions-31-2 for messaging-q012)

faq.q: Can you convert an existing standard queue to a FIFO queue?
faq.answer: No; you [choose the queue type when you create it] (sqs-faq-cannot-convert-standard-to-fifo), so create a new FIFO queue.
faq.quote: No. You must choose the queue type when you create it.

faq.q: Does a long-polling ReceiveMessage call cost more than a short-polling one?
faq.answer: No; long polls are [billed exactly the same] (sqs-faq-long-polling-no-extra-charge).
faq.quote: Long-polling ReceiveMessage calls are billed exactly the same as short-polling ReceiveMessage calls.

faq.q: Can a deleted message come back from a standard queue?
faq.answer: Rarely, yes: you might get a [previously-deleted message a second time] (sqs-faq-deleted-message-standard-may-repeat-fifo-never).
faq.quote: For standard queues, under rare circumstances, you might receive a previously-deleted message a second time.

faq.q: Can a queue share its messages with a queue in another Region?
faq.answer: No; each queue is [independent within each region] (sqs-faq-queues-are-independent-per-region).
faq.quote: Each Amazon SQS message queue is independent within each region.

faq.q: Can a FIFO queue use a standard queue as its dead-letter queue?
faq.answer: No; you [must use a FIFO dead letter queue] (sqs-faq-dlq-fifo-needs-fifo-standard-needs-standard) with a FIFO queue.
faq.quote: However, you must use a FIFO dead letter queue with a FIFO queue.

faq.q: Can you recall a message after you publish it to a topic?
faq.quote: No, once a message has been successfully published to a topic, it cannot be recalled.

faq.q: Can any AWS account publish to your topic by default?
faq.answer: No; by default [only topic owners have permissions to publish] (sns-faq-default-only-topic-owner-can-publish).
faq.quote: By default, only topic owners have permissions to publish to a topic.

faq.q: Does a standard SNS topic deliver messages in the order they were published?
faq.answer: Not always; SNS tries, but subscribers can see [out-of-order messages at the subscriber end] (sns-faq-order-attempted-but-network-issues-can-reorder). For order, use a FIFO topic.
faq.quote: However, network issues could potentially result in out-of-order messages at the subscriber end.

faq.q: Can EventBridge Scheduler call a third-party HTTPS endpoint directly?
faq.answer: No; it [does not support non-AWS targets directly] (eventbridge-faq-scheduler-no-direct-non-aws-targets). Use Lambda or the [API destinations feature] (eventbridge-faq-scheduler-no-direct-non-aws-targets).
faq.quote: EventBridge Scheduler does not support non-AWS targets directly.

faq.q: Can one EventBridge rule send an event to several targets?
faq.answer: Yes; a rule can [route to multiple targets] (eventbridge-faq-single-rule-routes-to-multiple-targets-in-parallel), all [processed in parallel] (eventbridge-faq-single-rule-routes-to-multiple-targets-in-parallel).
faq.quote: A single rule can route to multiple targets, all of which are processed in parallel.

question_slots.note: Shared stem of twin pair A (q01, q07): 'A company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 instances. The API writes each order directly to a relational database. During sales, the database cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost.' Ask: 'Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical in q01 and q07, in neutral words: (A) Send each order to an Amazon SQS queue. Have the order service poll the queue and write each order to the database. (B) Publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders. (C) Publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe the HTTPS endpoint of each service that processes orders. (D) Move the database to a larger instance class and add a read replica. Changed phrase of q01: 'Only the company's order service processes the orders. The order service must process every order, even after it has been offline for a few hours.' Key (A): the queue keeps each order [until successfully processed or expired] (sqs-decision-keeps-until-processed); [buffering requests] (sqs-decision-typical-use). (B) violates-qualifier: a topic adds a part when only one service consumes. (C) carries messaging-trap-topic-stores-messages: [Messages are not persisted] (sns-decision-no-persistence), and HTTP/S retries end after at most [3,600 seconds] (sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max). (D) misconception: a larger database does not keep orders while the order service is offline and still takes every write at the peak. Bullets also 2.1.S3, 2.1.K2.

question_slots.twin: first of strict twin pair B (twin q09)
question_slots.note: Shared stem of twin pair B (q02, q09): 'A company runs workers in an Auto Scaling group. The workers poll an Amazon SQS standard queue and delete each message after they process it.' Ask: 'Which change will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical: (A) Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to longer than the longest processing time. (B) Configure a dead-letter queue and a redrive policy for the queue. (C) Set the receive message wait time of the queue to 20 seconds. (D) Create a FIFO queue and move the producers and the workers to it. Changed phrase of q02: 'Processing a message takes up to 4 minutes. The queue uses the default visibility timeout, and many messages are processed by two different workers.' Key (A): the default [30 seconds] (sqs-visibility-timeout-default) ends while the first worker still works, so [a duplicate message is received by another consumer] (sqs-visibility-timeout-too-short-gives-duplicate). (B) misconception: a dead-letter queue sets failing messages aside; it does not stop a second receive. (C) misconception: long polling only waits for messages: [reduce the number of empty receives] (sqs-faq-long-polling-fewer-empty-receives-lower-cost). (D) violates-qualifier: you [cannot convert an existing standard queue] (sqs-cannot-convert-standard-queue-to-fifo), so it is a new queue and a migration, and a FIFO queue also returns a message whose visibility timeout ends. Bullets also 3.2.K3.

Difficulty 1, qualifier none (no violates-qualifier option). 'A consumer application receives a message from an Amazon SQS standard queue and processes it successfully. The application does not call DeleteMessage. The queue uses its default settings. What happens to the message?' Key: it becomes visible again when the visibility timeout ends, and a consumer receives it again ([becomes visible again in the queue] (sqs-undeleted-message-visible-again)). Distractors: SQS deleted it when the consumer received it (trap messaging-trap-receive-deletes; why links [temporarily invisible to other consumers] (sqs-receive-keeps-message-hidden)); SQS moves it to a dead-letter queue at once (misconception: only a redrive policy moves messages, after the [number of times a consumer can receive] (sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning)); it stays hidden until the retention period ends (misconception: it is hidden only for the visibility timeout). Bullets also 3.2.K3.

'A payment service reads orders from an Amazon SQS standard queue and charges the customer for each order. Sometimes a customer is charged twice for one order. The payment provider also retries some requests, and its duplicates can arrive hours apart. Which solution will BEST prevent duplicate charges?' Key: make the consumer idempotent: record each order ID with a conditional write and skip an ID that is already recorded ([keep track of each token received] (sqs-consumers-keep-idempotency-tokens-ignore-duplicates); [design your applications to be idempotent] (sqs-faq-standard-queue-design-idempotent-consumers)). Distractors: increase the visibility timeout to its maximum (misconception: copies on several servers also repeat a message: [more than one copy of a message] (sqs-standard-at-least-once-duplicates)); replace the queue with a FIFO queue with content-based deduplication (misconception: deduplication covers only the [5 minute deduplication interval] (sqs-fifo-deduplication-interval-5-minutes), and the provider's duplicates arrive later); keep the queue and only fix the provider integration, because a standard queue delivers each message once (trap messaging-trap-standard-exactly-once). The BEST qualifier: the key is the only option that covers both sources of duplicates. Bullets also 2.1.K11, 3.2.S1.

Difficulty 1, qualifier none. 'An order service must send each order event to three other microservices at the same time. Each microservice must receive every event. Which AWS service provides this publish/subscribe model?' Key: an Amazon SNS topic with one subscription for each microservice ([all applicable subscribers] (sns-faq-publish-triggers-delivery-to-all-subscribers)). Distractors: one Amazon SQS standard queue that the three microservices poll (trap messaging-trap-queue-broadcasts; why links [a single subscriber typically] (sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss)); an SQS FIFO queue with one message group for each microservice (misconception: each message still goes to one consumer); Amazon EventBridge Scheduler with one schedule for each microservice (misconception: a schedule starts work at set times; it does not forward events). Do not offer an EventBridge event bus as an option: a rule with several targets would also be right. Bullets also 2.1.K11.

'Whenever an Amazon EC2 instance in the account changes to the stopped state, the operations team must receive an email, and an existing AWS Lambda function must create a ticket. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?' Key: an EventBridge rule on the default event bus that matches EC2 state-change events with the state stopped, with two targets: an SNS topic that has an email subscription, and the Lambda function (the default bus [automatically receives events from AWS services] (eventbridge-default-bus-receives-aws-service-events); a rule can [route to multiple targets] (eventbridge-faq-single-rule-routes-to-multiple-targets-in-parallel)). Distractors: a Lambda function that runs every minute, calls DescribeInstances and compares states (violates-qualifier); an AWS CloudTrail trail to an S3 bucket with an S3 event notification that invokes a function that reads the logs (violates-qualifier); a shutdown script on every instance that publishes to an SNS topic (violates-requirement: it misses stops that the script does not see; keyword bait for 'event-driven': how-the-exam-asks-trap-keyword-bait only if the option text repeats a stem keyword). Bullets also 2.1.S3, 2.1.S1.

Shared stem of twin pair A (q01, q07): 'A company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 instances. The API writes each order directly to a relational database. During sales, the database cannot keep up, requests time out, and orders are lost.' Ask: 'Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical in q01 and q07, in neutral words: (A) Send each order to an Amazon SQS queue. Have the order service poll the queue and write each order to the database. (B) Publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for each service that processes orders. (C) Publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe the HTTPS endpoint of each service that processes orders. (D) Move the database to a larger instance class and add a read replica. Changed phrase of q07: 'The order service, the shipping service and the analytics service must each process every order. Each service must process every order, even after it has been offline for a few hours.' Key (B): subscribe [multiple SQS standard queues to the SNS topic] (sns-faq-fanout-identical-messages-to-multiple-sqs-queues), which prevents loss [when subscribers are offline] (sns-with-sqs-prevents-loss-for-offline-subscribers). (A) carries messaging-trap-queue-broadcasts: a queue has [a single subscriber typically] (sqs-typically-single-subscriber-order-and-loss). (C) carries messaging-trap-topic-stores-messages. (D) misconception as in q01. Bullets also 3.2.S1, 2.1.S1.

'A company processes images from an Amazon SQS queue with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Every message takes about the same time to process. The number of uploads changes during the day, and each image must be processed within a set time. The group uses target tracking on average CPU utilization, and messages often wait too long. Which metric should the target tracking policy use to BEST meet the processing-time goal?' Key: the backlog per instance, the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric divided by GroupInServiceInstances with metric math, with the acceptable backlog per instance as the target ([backlog per instance] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance); [GroupInServiceInstances] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-backlog-per-instance-metric-math)). Distractors: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible alone (trap auto-scaling-trap-queue-length-metric; why links [might not change proportionally] (ec2-auto-scaling-sqs-queue-length-not-proportional)); ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible (misconception: it counts in-flight messages: [received but not yet deleted or expired] (sqs-metric-not-visible-messages-is-in-flight)); NumberOfMessagesSent (misconception: it counts arrivals, not the wait). Worked think-aloud: find the constraint (the processing-time goal; load that changes), predict, eliminate, choose. Bullets also 3.2.S1.

Shared stem of twin pair B (q02, q09): 'A company runs workers in an Auto Scaling group. The workers poll an Amazon SQS standard queue and delete each message after they process it.' Ask: 'Which change will resolve this issue with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical: (A) Increase the visibility timeout of the queue to longer than the longest processing time. (B) Configure a dead-letter queue and a redrive policy for the queue. (C) Set the receive message wait time of the queue to 20 seconds. (D) Create a FIFO queue and move the producers and the workers to it. Changed phrase of q09: 'Processing a message takes a few seconds. A few malformed messages fail every time, and the workers receive them again and again for days.' Key (B): a redrive policy moves a message after the [number of times a consumer can receive] (sqs-dlq-max-receive-count-meaning) it; the dead-letter queue keeps messages the consumer is [unable to consume the messages successfully] (sqs-faq-dlq-definition-isolate-unprocessable-messages). (A) misconception: a longer timeout only spaces out the failures: [wait for a relatively long time] (sqs-visibility-timeout-too-long-delays-retry). (C) misconception. (D) violates-qualifier. Difficulty 1, qualifier none. 'A company wants to monitor an Amazon SQS queue and receive an alarm when messages wait too long before a consumer processes them. Which Amazon CloudWatch metric should the alarm use?' Key: ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage ([oldest unprocessed message in the queue] (sqs-metric-age-of-oldest-message-measures-lag)). Distractors: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible (misconception: in-flight messages); NumberOfMessagesSent (misconception: arrivals); CPUUtilization of the consumer instances (misconception: [100% CPU utilization is expected and should not be your primary metric] (ec2-auto-scaling-wa-queue-depth-metric-for-batch-work) for batch work). Bullets also 3.2.S1.

Select TWO, five options. 'A company sends account events for many customers to Amazon SQS. The events of each customer must be processed exactly once and in the order they were sent. Events of different customers must be processed in parallel by many consumers. Which TWO actions should a solutions architect take to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)' Keys: use an SQS FIFO queue ([exactly-once processing] (sqs-faq-fifo-exactly-once-processing)); set the message group ID to the customer ID (order [within a message group ID] (sqs-fifo-order-strict-within-group); [parallel processing of messages] (sqs-fifo-groups-processed-in-parallel)). Distractors: give each event a random message group ID, because a FIFO queue keeps the order of all events (trap messaging-trap-fifo-global-order; why links [may arrive or be processed out of order] (sqs-fifo-no-order-across-groups)); use one message group ID for all events (violates-requirement: no parallel work, because FIFO queues do not serve one group to [more than one consumer at a time] (sqs-faq-fifo-same-group-one-consumer-at-a-time)); use an SQS standard queue, which delivers each message once and in order (trap messaging-trap-standard-exactly-once). Bullets also 2.1.K11.

'An Amazon SNS topic receives every order event of a company, with a message attribute that holds the order type. Three Amazon SQS queues are subscribed. A Lambda function between the topic and the returns queue copies only return events into that queue. The company wants to remove the function with the LEAST development effort.' Key: subscribe the returns queue to the topic directly with a filter policy that matches the order type 'return' ([assign a filter policy to the topic subscription] (sns-filter-default-every-message)). Distractors: keep a function for filtering, because SNS sends every message to every subscriber (trap messaging-trap-filter-needs-function); create one topic for each order type and change the publishers (violates-qualifier); replace the topic with an EventBridge event bus and rules (violates-qualifier: publishers and consumers change). Bullets also 3.2.K3.
