question_slots.note: Shared stem of twin pair C (q13, q18): 'A company is building an event-driven platform. Several teams' services must react to events, and each service needs only some of the events.' Ask: 'Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical: (A) An Amazon EventBridge event bus with one rule for each service. (B) An Amazon SNS topic with a filter policy on each subscription. (C) One Amazon SQS queue that every service polls. (D) An Amazon Kinesis data stream that every service reads. Changed phrase of q13: 'The events come from AWS services, from the company's own applications and from a SaaS partner's application. Each service selects events by fields inside the event detail.' Key (A): EventBridge is the [only event-based service] (eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners) that integrates with [third-party SaaS partners] (eventbridge-faq-eventbridge-only-service-integrating-directly-with-saas-partners), and patterns test [event metadata, and/or event detail values] (eventbridge-pattern-matches-metadata-data-content). (B) violates-qualifier: AWS service and SaaS events would need EventBridge in front of the topic. (C) carries messaging-trap-queue-broadcasts. (D) misconception: a stream for [real-time processing of streaming big data] (sqs-faq-kinesis-streams-realtime-and-replay), with code in every reader. Bullets also 2.1.K5.

'A Lambda function reads an Amazon SQS standard queue with a batch size of 10. When one message of a batch is malformed, the function returns an error. The other nine messages are processed again and again, and at last all ten move to the dead-letter queue. Which solution will retry only the malformed message in the MOST operationally efficient way?' Key: turn on ReportBatchItemFailures and have the function return the IDs of the failed messages ([make only the failed messages visible again] (lambda-sqs-partial-batch-response)). Distractors: set the batch size to 1 (violates-qualifier: many more invocations); configure an on-failure destination or a dead-letter queue on the function (trap lambda-trap-function-dlq-for-sqs; why links [visibility timeout and redrive policy] (lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue)); lower the visibility timeout of the queue so that failures come back sooner (trap messaging-trap-short-visibility-safer). Bullets also 2.1.S1, 2.1.K5.

'An Amazon SQS standard queue and its dead-letter queue both keep the default retention period. Failed messages disappear from the dead-letter queue before the support team reviews them. The company must retain each failed message for at least 10 days after it was first sent. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?' Key: set the retention period of the dead-letter queue to 14 days ([14 days] (sqs-message-retention-range)), because [the enqueue timestamp is unchanged] (sqs-dlq-standard-enqueue-timestamp-unchanged) when a message moves. Distractors: set only the source queue's retention to 14 days (misconception: the dead-letter queue's own retention deletes the message; why links [longer than the retention period] (sqs-dlq-retention-longer-than-source-queue)); raise maxReceiveCount (misconception: the message stays longer in the source queue, but the clock still runs from the first send); have a scheduled Lambda function copy the dead-letter messages to Amazon S3 every day (violates-qualifier). Write the belief of the trap into the stem's situation, not into an option: the team assumed the move restarted the clock. Bullets also 2.1.K11.

'An Amazon SNS topic and an Amazon SQS queue are in the same AWS account. A developer subscribed the queue to the topic, and the subscription is active. Messages published to the topic never arrive in the queue. The queue has its default access policy. Which change will deliver the messages in the MOST secure way?' Key: add a statement to the queue's access policy that allows the SNS service principal to call sqs:SendMessage, with an aws:SourceArn condition that names the topic ARN ([set a policy on the Amazon SQS queue] (sns-sqs-queue-needs-policy-allowing-topic); [aws:SourceArn condition] (sns-queue-policy-sourcearn-limits-to-one-topic)). Distractors: allow every principal (*) to call sqs:SendMessage with no condition (violates-qualifier); confirm the subscription with ConfirmSubscription (misconception: a same-account queue subscription needs no [opt-in] (sns-faq-same-account-sqs-subscription-needs-no-opt-in)); keep the subscription and wait, because a subscription is all SNS needs (trap messaging-trap-subscribe-without-queue-policy). Bullets also 2.1.S3.

'A company publishes orders to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus. A rule sends them to a Lambda function. Last week a bug made the function process orders wrongly for several hours, and the company could not process those events again. After any future bug, the company must be able to process the events of the last 30 days again. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?' Key: create an archive of the bus that keeps events for 30 days, and after a fix start a replay of the affected time window ([reprocess past events] (eventbridge-faq-event-replay-reprocesses-past-events-to-bus-or-rule)). Distractors: read the past events again from the event bus (trap messaging-trap-bus-stores-events; why links [Not retained. To keep events, add an archive.] (eventbridge-classic-bus-does-not-retain-events)); add a dead-letter queue to the target (misconception: a dead-letter queue holds only events that could not be delivered, and these were delivered); add a rule that sends every event through Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon S3 and write a tool that publishes them again (violates-qualifier). Bullets also 2.1.S1.

Shared stem of twin pair C (q13, q18): 'A company is building an event-driven platform. Several teams' services must react to events, and each service needs only some of the events.' Ask: 'Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?' Options identical: (A) An Amazon EventBridge event bus with one rule for each service. (B) An Amazon SNS topic with a filter policy on each subscription. (C) One Amazon SQS queue that every service polls. (D) An Amazon Kinesis data stream that every service reads. Changed phrase of q18: 'All events come from the company's own order application. Every event must also reach the customers' mobile phones by SMS within seconds.' Key (B): SNS reaches [mobile applications, mobile phone numbers, and email addresses] (sns-a2p-subscriber-types) and suits [thousands or millions of endpoints] (sns-faq-sns-recommended-for-high-fan-out-thousands-or-millions); each service filters with [subscription filter policies] (sns-decision-filter-policies). (A) violates-qualifier: EventBridge targets do not include phone numbers, so a topic would be needed behind the rules (link the target list: [Lambda function (ASYNC)] (eventbridge-target-types-list) only if the why names targets). (C) carries messaging-trap-queue-broadcasts. (D) misconception. Bullets also 3.2.K3.

Select TWO, five options. 'An Amazon SNS standard topic delivers order events to a partner's HTTPS endpoint and to an Amazon SQS queue. The partner endpoint is sometimes down for several hours, and the events for the partner are lost. The company must keep the undelivered events so that it can send them again later. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)' Keys: create an SQS standard queue in the same AWS account and Region as the subscription ([same AWS account and Region] (sns-dlq-same-account-and-region-as-subscription)); set that queue as the dead-letter queue (redrive policy) of the HTTPS subscription ([attached to an Amazon SNS subscription] (sns-dlq-attached-to-subscription-not-topic)). Distractors: attach the dead-letter queue to the topic (trap messaging-trap-dlq-on-topic); use an SQS FIFO queue as the dead-letter queue ([standard topic subscriptions use standard queues] (sns-dlq-queue-type-matches-topic-type)); raise the HTTPS delivery retry policy to keep trying for 24 hours (impossible-feature: at most [3,600 seconds] (sns-retry-http-total-retry-time-max); the one impossible-feature option of the question). The topic keeps nothing itself: messaging-trap-topic-stores-messages may tag a fifth option 'rely on the topic to hold the events until the endpoint returns' if the writer uses it. Bullets also 2.1.S1, 2.1.K5.

'An application in account B runs with an IAM role. The role's policy allows sqs:SendMessage on an Amazon SQS queue in account A. Every call fails with an access denied error. The queue uses SSE-SQS. Which solution grants access MOST securely and follows the principle of least privilege?' Key: add a statement to the queue's access policy in account A that allows the role's ARN to call sqs:SendMessage on that queue ([configure the queue's access policy] (sqs-cross-account-needs-queue-access-policy)). Distractors: grant the role sqs:* on all resources in account B (trap messaging-trap-iam-policy-enough-cross-account; why links [aren't sufficient for cross-account access] (sqs-cross-account-needs-queue-access-policy)); allow every principal (*) in the queue policy (violates-qualifier); add the queue policy statement and remove the role's own policy (trap iam-trap-cross-account-one-policy; the why may link a chapter 03 fact on cross-account evaluation). The stem states SSE-SQS so that no key policy question arises. Bullets also 2.1.S3.

'A company must send a reminder email to each new user 3 days after the user signs up. Each reminder is a one-time action. The company wants a serverless solution with the LEAST operational overhead.' Key: when a user signs up, create an EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedule that invokes a Lambda function at the reminder time ([EventBridge Scheduler is the recommended solution] (sqs-eventbridge-scheduler-for-advanced-scheduling); a one-time schedule [invokes a target only once] (eventbridge-scheduler-one-time-schedule-invokes-once)). Distractors: send each reminder to an SQS delay queue with a 3-day delay (impossible-feature: at most [15 minutes] (sqs-delay-queue-range)); give each message a message timer of 3 days (misconception, same limit: [15 minutes] (sqs-message-timer-range); keep only one impossible-feature option, so label this one misconception); a cron job on an EC2 instance that checks the user table every hour (violates-qualifier). Bullets also 2.1.K5.

speak.prompt: SQS, SNS, EventBridge: all three move messages. When do I use which?
speak.note: Ben talks in short technical sentences and wants the fewest parts. Short answer: a queue when one consumer does the work at its own pace; a topic when every subscriber needs a copy now; EventBridge when AWS services or SaaS apps produce the events and rules pick them by content. How it works: SQS keeps a message until a consumer deletes it; SNS pushes copies and keeps nothing; an EventBridge rule matches events and sends them to up to five targets. Watch: SNS and EventBridge keep nothing, so put a queue behind them for any consumer that can be down. In your case: 'Which of your systems must keep working while another one is down?' Must not say: 'SNS stores messages until the subscriber is back'; 'one queue gives every service a copy'; 'an event bus keeps events for replay by default'. Numbers as words from the say forms: five targets.

speak.prompt: Our worker crashed in the middle of a job. Did we lose that message?
speak.note: Short answer: no, as long as the worker had not deleted it; it comes back when the visibility timeout ends. How it works: a receive hides the message, a delete removes it; the default timeout is thirty seconds; after several failed receives a redrive policy moves it to a dead-letter queue. Watch: the restart can process it twice, so the worker must be idempotent, and the timeout must be longer than the longest job. In your case: 'How long does your longest job take?' Must not say: 'the message is gone'; 'SQS delivers each message exactly once'; 'the dead-letter queue retries it for you'. Numbers as words from the say forms: thirty seconds.

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Standard queue or FIFO queue: which should we start with?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both keep messages safely; the difference is order and duplicates against throughput. Short answer: a standard queue, unless order per customer or no duplicates is a hard rule; then a FIFO queue with the customer ID as message group ID. How it works: a standard queue scales almost without limit but can repeat a message and change the order; a FIFO queue keeps order inside each group and drops duplicates, at a lower rate. Watch: you cannot turn a standard queue into a FIFO queue later; the type is chosen at creation. In your case: 'Does anything break if two events of one customer arrive out of order?' Must not say: 'standard queues keep the order'; 'a FIFO queue keeps one order across all customers'; 'you can switch to FIFO later'. No numbers (the FIFO rate facts have no spoken form).

speak.prompt: On launch day, uploads failed. What did we change so that it cannot happen again?
speak.note: Ana uses no AWS terms: explain a queue the first time as 'a waiting line for work that AWS keeps safe'. Short answer: an upload now waits safely in line instead of failing when the worker is busy. How it works: each upload is stored in several data centers before we say 'received'; workers take uploads from the line at their own pace; a recording that keeps failing is moved aside, so it blocks no one; when a transcript is ready, one message reaches both the customer webhooks and search. Watch: processing is not instant; customers see 'processing' for a while, and a message waits at most four days by default. In your case: 'How long may a customer wait for a transcript before we warn them?' Must not say: 'nothing can fail again'; 'transcripts are ready at once'; 'we fixed it with more servers'. Numbers as words from the say forms: four days.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, how long does a queue keep a message by default?
cards.back: 4 days.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, what is the longest message retention period?
cards.back: 14 days.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, what is the default visibility timeout?
cards.back: 30 seconds.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, what is the longest visibility timeout?
cards.back: 12 hours.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, how long can one long-polling call wait?
cards.back: 20 seconds.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, what is the longest delay of a delay queue?
cards.back: 15 minutes.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, how many messages per second does a FIFO queue support by default?
cards.back: 300 messages per second, or 3,000 messages per second with batching.

cards.front: In Amazon EventBridge, how many targets can one rule have?
cards.back: 5 targets.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, does receiving a message delete it?
cards.back: No. It stays in the queue, hidden from other consumers.

cards.front: Several services must each get every message. What do you build?
cards.back: An SNS topic with one SQS queue per service.

cards.front: In Amazon SNS, does a topic keep messages for an offline subscriber?
cards.back: No. Messages are not persisted; subscribe an SQS queue.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, can a standard queue deliver one message twice?
cards.back: Yes. Delivery is at least once; make consumers idempotent.

cards.front: Workers poll an SQS queue. Which metric should their Auto Scaling group track?
cards.back: Backlog per instance: visible messages divided by InService instances.

cards.front: In Amazon EventBridge, does a Classic event bus keep its events?
cards.back: No. To keep events, add an archive.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, what does a delay queue hide, and what does the visibility timeout hide?
cards.back: Delay: new messages. Visibility timeout: received messages.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, can you convert a standard queue to a FIFO queue?
cards.back: No. Create a new FIFO queue.

cards.front: In an SQS FIFO queue, do messages of different groups keep their order?
cards.back: No. They may arrive or be processed out of order.

cards.front: Each customer's events must stay in order, and customers must run in parallel. How?
cards.back: A FIFO queue with the customer ID as message group ID.

cards.front: In an SQS FIFO queue, what happens to a duplicate sent within the 5 minute deduplication interval?
cards.back: Only one copy is delivered.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, can a FIFO queue use a standard dead-letter queue?
cards.back: No. Its dead-letter queue must also be a FIFO queue.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, can a dead-letter queue be in another Region?
cards.back: No. Same AWS account and Region as the source queue.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, how long should a dead-letter queue keep messages?
cards.back: Longer than the retention period of the source queue.

cards.front: Lambda reads an SQS queue. How do you retry only the failed messages of a batch?
cards.back: Return a partial batch response with ReportBatchItemFailures.

cards.front: Lambda reads an SQS queue. How long should the queue's visibility timeout be?
cards.back: At least six times the function timeout.

cards.front: An SNS topic delivers nothing to a subscribed SQS queue. What is missing?
cards.back: A queue policy that allows the topic to send messages.

cards.front: One subscriber needs only some of a topic's messages. What do you add?
cards.back: A filter policy on that subscription.

cards.front: In Amazon SNS, where do you attach a dead-letter queue?
cards.back: To a subscription, not to the topic.

cards.front: A role in another account has an IAM policy for sqs:SendMessage. Is that enough?
cards.back: No. The queue's access policy must also allow it.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, can you edit the key policy of the AWS managed key?
cards.back: No. You cannot modify that key policy.

cards.front: In Amazon SQS, what is the difference between short polling and long polling?
cards.back: Short returns at once; long waits until a message arrives.

cards.front: A task must run once, three days from now. Which service schedules it?
cards.back: EventBridge Scheduler, with a one-time schedule.

cards.front: React to an EC2 state change without polling. What do you use?
cards.back: An EventBridge rule on the default event bus.
